title: Home Harvest, Drying and Storage as One Process

content.overview: Harvest quality can be lost after the plant is cut. Home growers should plan representative maturity observations, drying space, product-condition checks and storage before harvest day rather than improvising each step.

vocabulary.definition: Observation of multiple representative flower sites to characterize harvest development.
A measure related to how available water is for microbial growth and reactions.
How well defined quality attributes persist under a storage condition over time.

sections.title: Sample maturity, do not chase one trichome view
sections.body: Trichome development varies by genotype, age and position, so use multiple representative observations.

sections.title: Drying is product conditioning
sections.body: Temperature, humidity, airflow, flower size and loading influence drying and quality; elapsed days alone are not enough.

sections.title: Storage continues the quality timeline
sections.body: Light, oxygen, temperature, moisture and time can change cannabinoids and volatiles, so packaging and storage conditions matter.

workedExamples: If the crop is harvested before a suitable drying area is prepared, post-harvest control begins already compromised.
A sealed container does not correct material that entered storage too wet.
commonMistakes: Planning harvest but not drying capacity.
Using one flower to judge the whole plant.
Putting material into long-term storage without checking condition.
content.practicalApplication: Before harvest, write the maturity sampling plan, drying location/monitoring plan, expected product checks and storage container/location.
content.summary: Home harvest succeeds when maturity, drying and storage are planned as one connected quality process.
